title: Furniture demand planning: a practical guide for retailers
summary: Furniture demand planning starts from written orders, not deliveries. US furniture makers carried a $2.64bn order backlog in June 2026. Here is the method.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 26 October 2026.


Furniture demand planning is the monthly process of forecasting what customers will order (product, configuration, and location) and turning that forecast into purchase orders, production slots, and warehouse space far enough ahead to cover lead times of two to six months. It works when the plan starts from written orders instead of deliveries, decides product by product what to stock and what to make to order, and treats project sales as a separate stream.


Tom plans upholstery for a furniture retailer with 14 showrooms. For two years his forecast for a best-selling three-seat sofa was built on delivered units, because that is what the sales report showed. When the supplier's lead time stretched from eight to 14 weeks, deliveries fell for a quarter while showroom orders kept climbing, and the forecast read the delivery dip as falling demand. Tom cut the next container order, and by spring customers were quoted 20-week waits on the sofa that had never stopped selling. (Tom is an illustrative example, but planners in the category will recognize the loop.)


Most furniture planners know their lead times are long and their products are bulky. Turning that into a plan that a buyer and a warehouse manager can both work from is harder. This guide to furniture demand planning covers how demand behaves in the category, how to split stock from made-to-order products, a six-step monthly cycle, and how lead times and storage space change the numbers. To test the method on your own order history, you can[see how a forecast built on your written orders looks](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


> **Key Takeaways**
>
>
> - US furniture and home furnishings stores sold about $127 billion in 2025, and their strongest month (December, $11.2 billion) was only about 14% above the weakest (February, $9.8 billion), according to US Census Bureau monthly retail data, so lead times shape the plan more than seasonal peaks do.
> - Smith Leonard's Furniture Insights survey shows US residential furniture manufacturers with $2.64 billion in order backlog in June 2026, up 11% on a year earlier, against about $2.2 billion of monthly shipments.
> - In that same June 2026 survey, new orders rose 11% while shipments rose only 3%, which is the gap that makes delivered sales a lagging and misleading forecast input.
> - McKinsey found that early adopters of AI-enabled supply chain management improved inventory levels by 35% and service levels by 65% compared with slower competitors.
> - Safety stock grows with the square root of lead time, so a sofa on a 16-week lead time needs about a third more buffer than the same sofa on a 9-week lead time.


## What is furniture demand planning?


Furniture demand planning is the process of forecasting customer orders for each furniture product and configuration by channel and location, then converting that forecast into supplier orders, production capacity, and warehouse space over a horizon that covers the full lead time. It sets which products are stocked, which are made to order, and how much of each to commit.


The unit of the plan is wider than in most retail categories. A sofa in three sizes, four fabrics, and two leg finishes is 24 possible configurations, and a retailer that offers custom fabric has hundreds more. Planning works when the forecast is built at the level where the stocking decision is made (often the frame and size for made-to-order lines, and the full configuration for stocked ones) and then rolls up. That is the logic behind[demand planning software that forecasts at product and location level](https://www.metreecs.com/demand-planning) .


Furniture shares a lot with home décor, and our guide to[demand forecasting for home décor retailers](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/demand-forecasting-home-decor-retailers) covers the variant-level forecast for accessories, lighting, and textiles in depth. This article stays on the planning cycle that is specific to furniture: orders that ship weeks after they are written, products that are only built once sold, and stock that is measured in floor space as much as in units.


## Why furniture demand planning differs from other home categories


Five features of furniture push a standard retail plan off course, and each one changes how furniture demand planning has to be set up.


**Orders and deliveries are two different curves.** A customer orders a dining table in March and receives it in May. If the forecast learns from deliveries, every change in lead time shows up as a fake change in demand. Furniture manufacturers already track this split: Smith Leonard's monthly survey reports new orders, shipments, and backlog as three separate figures, and in June 2026 orders grew 11% while shipments grew 3%.


**Seasonality is mild, and lead time dominates instead.** Census data shows a gap of about 14% between the best and worst month for US furniture stores in 2025, far flatter than gift categories such as jewelry, so furniture demand planning spends less effort on peak profiles and more on timing. Promotions around holiday weekends still move volume, but the bigger planning risk is ordering too late for a lead time that has just stretched.


**A large share of demand is made to order.** Many retailers sell upholstery, dining, and bedroom furniture from a showroom sample, with production starting after the sale. For those products the forecast drives fabric, frames, and production slots rather than finished stock.


**Products are bulky, so space is a constraint.** A boxed sofa takes the floor space of dozens of small home products, and a warehouse fills by volume long before it fills by unit count. Overstock in furniture costs storage space, handling, and damage risk, and the plan has to show stock in cubic meters as well as in units.


**Project demand arrives in large blocks.** Hotel refits, office fit-outs, and property developers order hundreds of identical pieces at once. Left in the retail history, one project looks like a demand spike that the model then tries to repeat.


In our experience deploying product-level forecasting at Metreecs, furniture planners often underestimate how much of their forecast error comes from mixing written and delivered sales in the same history. Fixing the input data usually does more for accuracy than changing the forecasting method.


## Stock or made to order: decide product by product


The stock versus made-to-order decision is the first lever in furniture demand planning, and it should be made per product, not per company. Two questions drive it: how predictable is demand for the exact configuration, and how long will a customer wait for it?


Approach Pros Cons Ideal use case


Stock finished configurations Fast delivery, sales not lost to long waits Ties up cash and floor space, markdown risk on slow fabrics and finishes Best-selling configurations with steady weekly demand


Make to order Little finished stock, wide choice for the customer Long waits, cancellations, demand hidden in the backlog Custom fabrics, large or premium pieces, low-volume configurations


Stock components, assemble or finish to order Shorter waits than full make to order, less finished stock Needs a forecast for frames, fabrics, and parts Upholstery ranges with many fabric options on a few frames


Hybrid (stock the top configurations, make the rest to order) Balances speed and choice Needs a clear rule for which configurations move between groups Mid-market retailers with large showroom ranges


A simple rule many furniture planners use: rank configurations by unit sales over the last 12 months, stock the ones that account for most of the volume, and sell the long tail to order. Review the cut-off every quarter, because a fabric that moves into the top group needs to be stocked before customers start waiting for it.


Ines runs planning for a direct-to-consumer furniture brand that sells dining chairs in 18 fabric and frame combinations. All 18 were stocked, and six of them sold fewer than two units a month. She moved those six to made to order with a six-week promise, kept the top 12 in stock, and used the freed warehouse space for a second color of the best-selling table. (Ines is an illustrative example.) Her plan now carries two forecasts per chair: finished units for the stocked group and fabric meters for the made-to-order group.


## A monthly furniture demand planning cycle in six steps


This cycle runs once a month, with a weekly check on orders. It assumes at least two years of order history with order date, delivery date, configuration, and channel.


1. **Rebuild demand from written orders.** Use the order date, not the delivery date, as the demand signal. Remove cancellations, and tag project and trade orders so they can be planned separately.
2. **Split the range into stock and made-to-order groups.** Apply the product-by-product rule above. Stocked configurations get a unit forecast; made-to-order lines get a forecast at frame or model level plus a mix of fabrics and finishes.
3. **Forecast retail demand by product family and channel.** Group products that sell in a similar pattern (for example, all three-seat sofas in one price band), forecast the family, then split to configurations by recent share. Add planned promotions and showroom openings as explicit adjustments with a written reason.
4. **Plan project demand as a pipeline.** Pull quoted projects from the sales team with a probability and an expected order month. Commit materials and capacity for the projects that are signed, and hold a provisional slot for the ones that are likely.
5. **Convert the forecast into orders and production slots.** For each stocked configuration, order to cover forecast demand over the lead time plus the review period, plus safety stock, minus stock on hand and on order. For made-to-order lines, book fabric and production capacity against the model forecast.
6. **Check the plan against space and cash.** Translate the incoming stock into cubic meters per warehouse and per month, and into purchase value. If a month overflows, move the order date or the delivery point before the containers ship.


A monthly furniture demand planning review then compares the forecast with written orders, by family, and tracks bias separately from error. This cycle fits naturally into a wider sales and operations process, and our article on[sales and operations planning software](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/sales-and-operations-planning-software) covers how the demand review connects to supply and finance.


## Lead times, containers and bulky storage in furniture demand planning


The planning horizon in furniture demand planning has to cover the full lead time plus the time between two orders. If a sofa takes 12 weeks from order to the warehouse and you order every four weeks, you need a forecast you can trust 16 weeks out. Imported case goods with ocean transit often need a longer view still.


Lead time also sets the size of the buffer. With the standard formula, safety stock equals a service factor times the standard deviation of weekly demand times the square root of the lead time in weeks. Take a stocked sofa with a weekly demand standard deviation of 3 units and a 95% service target (factor 1.65):


- On a 9-week lead time: 1.65 × 3 × 3 = about 15 units of safety stock.
- On a 16-week lead time: 1.65 × 3 × 4 = about 20 units of safety stock.


(These figures are our own illustrative arithmetic.) Five extra sofas look small on paper, but in floor space they can take as much room as a full bay of small home products. For the full method behind these buffers, see our guide to[optimizing safety stock](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/safety-stock-optimization) .


Containers add a second constraint to furniture demand planning. Suppliers often want full containers, so the order quantity is set by volume rather than by the forecast for each product. A good plan fills the container with the configurations that are closest to running out, rather than topping it up with whatever is cheapest to ship.


Kofi plans for a furniture retailer that also sells to hotels. A 220-room refit asked for bedside tables, desks, and chairs, to be delivered in two waves over four months. Kofi kept the order out of the retail forecast, booked production for the signed first wave, and held a provisional slot for the second wave until the client confirmed it. When the second wave slipped by six weeks, the retail plan for the same desk was unaffected, and he had no excess stock to clear. (Kofi is an illustrative example.)


## Where furniture demand planning falls short


A plan narrows uncertainty without removing it, and three gaps stay open in furniture.


- **Custom and one-off pieces.** A bespoke dining table has no forecast in any useful sense. Plan capacity and materials for the custom range as a whole instead of each piece.
- **Sudden lead time shocks.** Port congestion, supplier failures, or tariff changes can add weeks overnight. A forecast cannot predict them, but a plan built on written orders shows the effect quickly, and agreed scenarios (normal, plus four weeks, plus eight weeks) speed up the response.
- **Large projects that change late.** Contract orders move with the client's own schedule. Keep them in a separate pipeline with probabilities, and avoid committing finished stock for the unsigned part.


Across Metreecs' work with home and furniture retailers, the plans that hold up are the ones where buying, sales, and the warehouse look at the same numbers in units and in volume. One mistake we repeatedly see is a stock versus made-to-order split decided once at range launch and never revisited, which leaves slow configurations in stock and fast ones on a long wait.


## FAQ


### How do furniture retailers forecast demand?


Furniture demand planning starts from written orders by order date, with cancellations removed and project orders tagged separately. Planners forecast at product family level, split to configurations by recent sales share, and add promotions and showroom openings as explicit adjustments. The forecast is reviewed monthly against new orders, not against deliveries.


### Should a furniture store stock products or sell them made to order?


Most retailers do both, and the split is the first decision in furniture demand planning. Stock the configurations that make up most of the volume and sell steadily, and offer the long tail of fabrics, sizes, and finishes made to order. Review the split every quarter so that rising configurations move into stock before waits get long.


### How far ahead should furniture retailers plan?


Furniture demand planning should cover at least the lead time plus the review period. With a 12-week supplier lead time and monthly orders, that is about 16 weeks of reliable forecast. Imported products with long ocean transit need a longer horizon, and project demand needs a pipeline view of several months.


### How do you plan inventory for furniture with long lead times?


In furniture demand planning, size safety stock with the lead time, because the buffer grows with the square root of the weeks covered. Check the plan in cubic meters as well as units, so the warehouse does not overflow when several containers land in the same month. When lead times change, update the order dates first, before the forecast.


### How do you forecast special orders and custom furniture?


Forecast them at model or frame level, then plan the materials (fabric meters, frames, finishes) and production capacity they will need. Custom orders show up in the backlog before they ship, so tracking open orders by order date gives the earliest read on demand.


## Conclusion


Furniture demand planning works when it starts from written orders, splits stocked and made-to-order products deliberately, keeps project demand in its own pipeline, and checks every plan against lead time and warehouse space. A good first step is to rebuild last year's demand by order date and compare it with delivered sales, because the gap usually shows where the plan has been misreading demand.
